# Diagnosing Indicator Failures on the Nissan Wingroad (2004)

When a vehicle's indicators cease functioning while the hazard lights operate normally, it is often an electrical architecture issue rather than a simple component failure. In the case of the 2004 Nissan Wingroad, the distinction between these two functions lies in how the signals are routed through the fuse box and the flasher relay. If you are troubleshooting this specific model, understanding the difference between a dedicated circuit and a shared ground is critical to avoiding unnecessary part replacements.

The symptoms describedâfunctional headlights, tail lights, and hazard indicators alongside dead directional signalsâpoint directly to a specific circuit failure. The hazard lights work because they bypass the standard indicator logic; they typically bridge both left and right circuits simultaneously through a separate relay or internal switch position within the multi-function stalk. When you engage the turn signal, the system expects current to flow from the battery, through the fuse, to the flasher unit, and out to the bulbs. If that path is broken, the circuit remains dead even if the rest of the lighting system is intact.

Your initial suspicion regarding a blown fuse is technically sound. However, visual inspection alone is insufficient for fuses rated at 10A or lower, especially in older vehicles where heat exposure can degrade the plastic casing without melting the internal wire. The images provided show two distinct locations: one near the battery and another in an interior panel. On many Nissan platforms of this era, the primary fuses are located under the dashboard, often requiring removal of a trim panel to access the main fuse box shown in your second photo.

The specific fuse for the indicators is not always explicitly labeled "TURN SIGNAL" or "INDICATOR." Instead, manufacturers frequently group these circuits under broader labels like "ECU," "ACC," or generic amperage ratings if they share a common feed. Based on standard wiring diagrams for the J10 generation Wingroad, the indicator circuit often shares a fuse with other accessories or is protected by a specific blade fuse located in the interior box near the battery.

Do not assume that because the ECU and TAIL LAMP fuses appear intact, the entire electrical system is fine. A blown fuse can sometimes look normal if the internal metal element has fractured but the plastic housing remains unbroken. The definitive diagnostic step involves using a multimeter to measure continuity across the fuse terminals with the ignition off. If there is no continuity, replace the fuse immediately.

If replacing the suspected fuse restores function, you have identified the root cause. However, if the new fuse blows instantly upon turning on the indicators, the issue has moved beyond the fuse box. You are likely dealing with a short circuit in one of the indicator bulbs or the wiring harness running to the flasher unit. Before concluding that the flasher relay is at fault, ensure you have isolated the bulb side of the circuit. Swapping the flasher relay with a known good unit from another vehicle is a quick test that can confirm whether the issue is electronic or purely resistive.

It is also worth noting that in some configurations, the indicator fuse might be labeled under a different name entirely, such as "PWR" or "IGN," depending on how the factory grouped the power distribution. Always cross-reference the fuse box lid diagram with the vehicle's specific service manual if available, as labeling can vary by trim level.
